utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, you'll first be examined by Ms. MacGregor. You'll find her to your right. Ms. MacGregor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My name is Fredy Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I see that you have brought into the courtroom some materials. Can you please let the Chamber know what you have there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a new copy of Mr. Peccerelli's CV which we received last night. We've e-mailed it to the Defence. There's currently not a B/C/S translation, although we will get one. Oh. Excuse me, Your Honours, the number is 30433.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, as we wait for that document to load, I'll ask you to just identify what the document is for the Chamber once you see it on your screen.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution first seeks to add this document to its 65 ter list and then to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And we no longer need that document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, you have testified before at this Tribunal as an expert about your work conducting excavations on what are known as the Lazete graves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I have testified three previous times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And were those in the trials of Popovic, Tolimir, and Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review the statement which the Prosecution is tendering for you today, which is parts of your Tolimir and Karadzic testimony?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please show 65 ter 04589; e-court page 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And, Court Officer, I'll don't think we'll need the B/C/S version since I'm just focussing on the pictures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on the lower of the three pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you see that picture, Mr. Peccerelli, you described in your testimony a wire ligature around the person's leg. Is that description correct of what we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect. This is, in fact, a ligature using a -- a piece of material. There is, however, a wire ligature in one of the previous two photographs, and I must have been mistaken when I mentioned that it was this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And we no longer need the picture on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Including the correction we've just made, is this testimony -- was the testimony you gave in Tolimir and Karadzic true to the best of your knowledge, when you gave it?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And would you give the same answers, in substance, if you were asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution seeks leave to add the 92 ter statement of this witness to its 65 ter exhibit list, as well as a very brief table of concordance which shows which exhibit numbers in the previous cases correlate with the exhibit numbers in our case, and I can provide those 65 ter numbers when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, you started by saying "seeks leave to add..." and then you said that's a 92 ter statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: My understanding was that the -- when we took the transcript excerpts and had to give them a 65 ter number which wasn't previously on the Prosecution's exhibit list as submitted at the beginning of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Leave is granted. Could you please give then the -- provide the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. The Tolimir excerpt has 65 ter 30418. And the excerpt from Mr. Peccerelli's Karadzic testimony has 65 ter number 30419. And, finally, the table of concordance is 30420. At this stage, Your Honour, may I please read a summary briefly of Mr. Peccerelli's evidence into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You seek admission of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry. I seek admission of the two excerpts and the table of concordance which were just added to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then since there are no objections, 30418 receives number...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you give me a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours -- oh, excuse me. Your Honours, I'm informed by Ms. Stewart that they've been released into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, for the first one, 30418.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still cannot see them. It will take some time but, if you wish, I can assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with that -- we'll deal with that in a second once all the technicalities are completed. Ms. MacGregor, you asked whether you could read the summary. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Peccerelli is a forensic pathologist. He worked for the ICTY on the excavation and exhumation of mass graves from 1997 through 2000. In 2000, he held the position of deputy senior director of the archaeology team under Professor Richard Wright. He was responsible for finding a grave, recovering its contents, ensuring the chain of custody, and placing human remains recovered from the grave in a refrigerated container to be send to the morgue in Visoko. In 2000, Mr. Peccerelli, headed the team-working on the Lazete 1 mass grave. The grave contained 127 bodies and two further bodies were found in an adjacent ditch. Eighty-nine of the bodies had probable blindfolds. It was clear that the bodies had previously been removed from the grave, since in some places the team only found body parts and the soil was different from the rest of the grave. The same year, 2000, Mr. Peccerelli, also supervised the excavation of the part of the Lazete 2 grave which was very nearby. This grave had previously been excavated in 1996 by a team from Physicians for Human Rights, or PHR, led by Dr. Bill Haglund. In addition to the 1996 PHR excavation, it was clear that bodies had been previously removed from the Lazete 2 grave in a robbing event, since in someplace, the team only found body parts and there were truncated bodies at the edge of the robbing areas. Mr. Peccerelli's team recovered 16 bodies from the grave as well as body parts and a large number of artefacts mostly comprising shell casings. Mr. Peccerelli completed reports on these excavations for the OTP. Your Honours, if I may put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, in the summary I just provided I provided to two reports which the Prosecution is tendering, your report on Lazete 1 and Lazete 2. Did you happen -- have an opportunity to review these two reports before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you still stand by the analysis and the conclusions of these reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Before you worked for the OTP in 2000, did you have prior experience or training with mass grave excavations?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. I started working in the exhumation of mass graves in 1995 in Guatemala. At that time we were exhuming graves of similar size as a result of the internal armed conflict in Guatemala.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did have any prior experience --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. The court reporter is asking to you pause between question and answer and the next question, and to slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, I should have asked at the beginning and reminded both of us as we both speak English. Did you have prior experience in Bosnia with mass grave excavations before 2000?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in the 1997 exhumations of Brcko, as well as in 1998 I participated in the exhumations of several sites related to the Srebrenica case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Specifically relating to Lazete 1 and 2, were you present for the duration of those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I was present the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you drafted these two reports for the Office of the Prosecutor, what sources of your own did you review in order to write the reports?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I had field notes, digital images, as well as copies of the site logs and of the skeletal sheets that we used to exhume all the bodies, body parts and artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you review or use sources from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I did not. Well, let me, I guess, clarify that. As part of the team, there was a Ian Hanson, who was a surveyor, so he was doing some of the, I guess, drawings that are shown in both reports at my request.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders into evidence the two reports, Lazete 1, and Lazete 1, completed by Mr. Peccerelli. I can provide those 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first go back to the previous numbers which are now - let me see - 30418. Madam Registrar, receives...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2549, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Then 65 ter 30419.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2550, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the last one, 30420.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The 65 ter number for report on Lazete 1 is 04589. The 65 ter number for Lazete 2 report is 11044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. 04589, Madam Registrar, receives number...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2552, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And admitted into evidence. 65 ter 11044.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P2553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If the Court Officer can please show Exhibit P2552, e-court page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, while this loads, I've asked them to show the cover of your Lazete 1 report. And this, again, it is sufficient to show just the English version since I'm going to be focussing on the photograph. Mr. Peccerelli, looking at the photo in front of you, can you describe what we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. This is an aerial photograph that was taken by our photographer, Tim Loveless, during a helicopter flight over the Lazete 1 site while we were conducting the excavation. You can actually see the site which lies between the road, the main road, and train tracks. The main road would be on the left, if you look at the picture straight ahead, and the train tracks would be on the right. There's also a dirt track that goes from the main road and then underneath the train tracks, that then turns right into another dirt road, and there's a clearing in the right bottom part of the picture. That clearing is where we later began the surface recovery and excavation procedures for the location of Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And to be clear, can you identify where the Lazete 1 excavation is happening in this picture?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. May I use a pointer?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I can -- it's actually easier if you can describe for the record.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Okay. On the main road and where the dirt track turns to the right about dead centre in this picture, there is soil movements that are different in colour from the surrounding area. You can see planted fields all around it, and some tree lines, but within this area where you can see are some vehicles, some light-coloured brown soil, and in the middle of that you see an oval shape hole. That oval shape hole is the Lazete 1 grave and it lies between the road, the main road, just below the dirt track and to the left of the train tracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please turn to page 12 in this same document, e-court page 12, and zoom in on the picture at the top of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, according to your report, these are also aerial images of the same area. Can you orient us in this picture using a reference to the railroad and where it is located in this picture so we are oriented similarly to how you oriented us in the last picture?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, this is actually two different images of the same field, and the difference between the previous and this one is that they're both -- they're both turned slightly to the right. The train track would be the white line that cuts across slightly off centre in the right bottom part. It's very clear. It's very straight. One image has the date of 5th of July, 1995, and the other image has a date of the 27th of July, 1995. Where the 5th of July label stands is where -- right underneath the 1995 is where we found the location of Lazete 1 grave, and in the lower right quadrant just off a small dirt track that runs parallel and to the right of the train tracks is where we found the Lazete 2 grave. On the picture on the left, you don't see any disturbance. This picture was shown to me by ICTY investigators, and they also gave me the picture on the right, the image on the right, which shows an oval-shaped lighter colour pointed to as Lazete 1. This was a disturbance that occurred between the 5th of July and the 27th of July. And there's also another disturbance just below to the right of the train tracks, a much larger disturbance. What these are, actually soil movements. That's why they show a different colour in the imagery, and this is also pointed as -- that is pointed as Lazete 2 [Realtime transcript read in error "1"] grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please turn to e-court page 14 of this same document and, again, it's the photograph that I want to look at so it can be just the English version. If you can zoom in actually on the second photograph rather than the top, it is actually a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask for one clarification. The last sentence of your answer, Mr. Peccerelli, is recorded as, "This also pointed as Lazete 1 grave." If I'm not mistaken you said "Lazete 2 grave."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. I did say Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According to your report, this picture on your screen now, Mr. Peccerelli, is 127 bodies found when you dug into the Lazete 1 grave. Now, why are the bodies left in place rather than removed as each body is discovered?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We used instances that we -- as we exhume, we remove layer by layer in reverse order of deposit. In other words, what you are seeing here are the last bodies to be put in this grave. And the first bodies to be put in this grave would be in the bottom. What we do is uncover the entire grave so we can understand the layout and so that we can make assessments as far as when or if these bodies were deposited in a single event. Are there cuts into the grave that would allow us to make determinations of why the bodies are in such an odd formation, as well as understanding the entire layout of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: To be clear for the record, I think what you said was stratographic methodology; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Stratographic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir -- sir, sorry, I'm getting very bad feedback in my mike -- in my earphones. I'll just stay it like this. Is there any effect to the decomposition of the bodies to leave them exposed as they are in this picture, to the air?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. Because these bodies have been buried for several years, once the grave is open, decomposition will accelerate. There was a mixture of decomposition. There was skeletonisation and saponification, both on this grave. So what happens, for example, is the saponified tissue or adipocere will begin to dry and become brittle on the bodies exposed to the sunlight, but all it does is attract or creates a foul odour and attracts some insects. This will not, however, have a long-term effect on the -- on the skeletal remains and the exposure was limited to several days, not to several weeks or months.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You've used the word saponification. If you can just in lay terms explain what that means, please.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, saponification is a decomposition stage whereas the traditional way a body decomposes would be through putrefaction. In other words, the tissues become liquified through insect activity and other factors. In adipocere formation or saponification, what you have is the tissues turning into fat. In other words, the fat becomes this white-ish lardy [Realtime transcript read in error "hardy"] substance, sometimes -- I mean, if you look up the word saponification it literally means to turn into soap, so it's termed sort of as grave grease in lay terms. But it a stage that usually is accompanied by very humid environments and we see it here on some of the bodies, and some of the bodies, at least the bodies on the outer edges, are more skeletonised and less susceptible to this type of decomposition which we found to be normal in many of the graves in this region.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- you used a word at line 18. It's captured in the transcript as "hardy." I think what you said was "lardy," as in like lard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is what I meant. I meant lardy, lard. I don't know if lardy is a word but lard in the idea of a waxy, wax substance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. My final question is also related to the different types of decomposition, and it relates -- if the Court Officer can actually bring up the Lazete 2 report which has exhibit number 30 -- excuse me, P2550. Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lazete 2 report is P2553.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. E-court page 19. And, again, we're just looking at the picture in the -- in this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: As this loads, Mr. Peccerelli, according to your report, you state that it's probable that the bodies shown in this picture were truncated during a grave robbing and you've talked about different types and forms and methods of decomposition. Why is it that you conclude that this body has been truncated by some activity rather than that this same body may have been exposed to different types or rates of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Okay. One of the main facts that we used to determine that these bodies were at the edges of the robbing was the fact that they were truncated. In other words, the bodies were separated from the rest of the body. These body parts, let's say. They were cut via very abrupt forces that ripped the rest of the body from this portion of the body. The bodies are skeletonised here. But, once again, I must refer to the fact that each body decomposes differently even within a grave. However, these bodies were at the edge of the robbing and we must remember that one of the factors that influences decomposition is depth or the availability of the body to aerobic bacteria. So being close to these edges of the robbing area could have exposed these bodies to a faster decomposition. However, that is not the point in these images. More the point is to understand that this grave was altered and that bodies that lay there -- initially parts of bodies that lay there initially and probably bodies that lay there as well, were removed and taken elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready -- Mr. Peccerelli, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading your biography I found there that as early as 1995 you were involved in the activities of the Foundation of Forensic Anthropology in Guatemala and that at the same time, you established the first forensic genetics laboratory in Guatemala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved as early as 1995, but the forensic genetics laboratory was not established till November of 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that your professional training and work experience includes both branches of forensic -- forensic science, anthropological and genetic?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My studies are in forensic anthropology and in practicing forensic anthropology in Guatemala I noticed a great deficiency in having the availability of technology used for human identification. That is why I began in the year 2000 to write proposals to bring this type of technology to Guatemala, and, in doing so, I have had some training as I state also in my CV, but I do not consider myself an expert in genetics. I -- as executive director, I do hired experts in genetics. However, I do oversee all identifications at the FAFG. Since we do not consider identifications to be only based on one aspect, they are multi-disciplinary identifications where we must check not only the result from the investigations of victims and their families but also the archaeology, the anthropology and the genetics to understand an entire case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The laboratory you spoke about in Guatemala was it accredited, and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. The Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology DNA Laboratory is accredited under international standards, organisation rule 170252005. It is accredited by the office, the Guatemalan Office of Accreditation, which belongs to the Ministry of Economics in Guatemala. But what it does is it -- it audits the FAFG to make sure that all of -- is administrative as well as scientific procedures are mapped up to the standard of this rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to acquaint yourself with the experiences and the work of the ICMP which is a similar laboratory in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Our laboratory or the installation of our laboratory in Guatemala led us to look at other experiences. One of them was the identification of the victims of the World Trade Centre in New York and the other was the experience of the ICMP in the Balkans. One of the things that I did was I hired Mr. John Cruise [phoen] who had worked for ICMP during implementation stage of its laboratories in Bosnia and later went on to work to -- for the Bode Technology Group, a laboratory in Virginia in the United States that worked on the identifications of the victims of the World Trade Centre. So what I was looking for was the experience of establishing a laboratory as well as having technical experience in extracting DNA from bone, and Mr. John Cruise had this experience by working both in Bosnia and in the World Trade Centre case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the laboratory in Guatemala you spoke about registered as a state-owned or public organisation or as a non-profit organisation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The laboratory is registered under the Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology Foundation which is a non-governmental organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the ICMP in Bosnia and Herzegovina, is it also registered as an NGO to the extent of your knowledge and taking into consideration the level of your co-operation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: To my knowledge, I don't know how ICMP is registered within Bosnia. I have participated in several meetings with some ICMP members, and I understand that it was formed by several states and it has an international organisation standing, from what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move onto another topic, namely, the procedures and protocols in your work. Having been hired to work in Bosnia by the OTP of the ICTY, did you acquaint yourself with the procedures to obey while exhuming and excavating grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Although I worked for ICMP -- I mean, I'm sorry, ICTY, my understanding was in 2000, at least, that I had technical control of the investigation, and in no time did anyone at ICTY or the OTP interfere with the technical control. I was instructed, however, where I should work but not how I should work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that upon arriving at the Lazete grave-site you had previously prepared procedures you were supposed to comply with while working on those two grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I was part of the initial ICTY exhumation team in 1997, when Professor Richard Wright first took over the role of senior forensic archaeologist for ICTY. Together, he and the rest of the team, we came to a consensus of the procedures that we should be using to exhume these graves. These are the procedures that were used in all of the excavations and they were altered or changed, according to the necessity of each one of these investigations. But, in theory, they remained pretty much the same, whereby we had a clear idea of how things should be done on the site. And I also had a clear idea in 2000 that, if necessary, I could change some of that methodology according to the necessity of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now get from e-court P2553, page 7 in both languages. Please focus on chapter 5, the first paragraph of that chapter, where you say that Richard Wright wrote a guide-line for the excavation of bodies, body parts and artefactual evidence during ICTY exhumations. Then you say: "I briefly revised and adopted these general exhumation procedure... for the excavation and exhumation of LZ02C. A copy of these procedures was given to each of the archaeologists and anthropologists prior to the excavation and exhumation." My first question is in what your revision of these procedures consists?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't recall if we changed any procedures. I mean, revised can also mean to check, to look over, and if the initial procedures were sufficient, then we didn't change anything. I would have to look at each one of these and the original to try to determine if we changed anything. Lazete 2 was a very complex exhumation, and one of the things that we changed, as far as the methodology went, is that we started this site while Lazete 1 was still going on. So what I would do is I would go back and forth. We did not assign a person to be at the grave-site till we were finished with Lazete 1. However, we did have an archaeologist on site the entire time as we were also recording the surface finds. I am guessing it was along those lines but I would have to review it very carefully and line by line against the original sites, again, like I said. And it's stated there these initial procedures were written in 1997 and they were found to be very useful and methodologically adequate, and there was an evolution of these throughout the years but I can't think of anything off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me then phrase my question differently. When you read your report by which you stand, would you say that this revision and adoption only applied to Lazete 1 rather than Lazete 1. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. When I read my report, it's -- the report is saying what we used, not what it was changed from. What it was changed from in either case it was not recorded. More than that, what was recorded is what we used in each specific case. From my recollection, I don't think there was much variation between Lazete 1 and Lazete 2 methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you the following. According to you, is Professor Snow a person of undisputed authority in your line of work?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Professor Clyde Snow is the single individual that we attribute the application of forensic anthropology techniques to the investigation of mass human rights abuses. He started in 1984 in Argentina, then later in 1987 in Chile, and then later in 1991 and 1992 in Guatemala. Dr. Clyde Snow happens to be my mentor and we have a very close relationship as he is one of the advisors, permanent advisors of the FAFG, so I do hold him in very high standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to acquaint yourself with the fact that he, as a high authority in your line of work, was also involved in exhumations in former Yugoslavia, or more specifically Bosnia and Herzegovina at one point?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I know of Clyde's -- or Dr. Snow's involvement in the Balkans in a site -- I'm trying to remember the name. In a site in Croatia, if I'm not mistaken, by a hospital. I don't know of any sites that he worked in Bosnia. I might be mistaken. Vukovar. There you go. Vukovar was the name of the site that I know that he worked and that he mentioned to me. But that's the only case that he's ever mentioned to me in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already been asked in early trials about the San Antonio report which is a summary of a scientific conference from November 1997. Let me ask you if you inquired into the results or conclusions of that conference concerning the methodology and protocols used in the work in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I was asked about this San Antonio report previously, and as I answered previously, I have never seen it or know exactly what it pertains to. I've never read it. So I really don't know what it -- what it specifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind then to take a look at some of the excerpts and I would like to hear your opinion regarding the procedures that you applied as the basis in your work in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, before we move on to this specific subject, maybe we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take that break. But could we first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I gained the impression that we're now slowly moving to an issue after 20 minutes. Whereas, I have -- I would be surprised if some of the matters you raised are really in dispute. For example, ESO accreditation. All that. I mean, did we really need all that in order to now come close to apparently what seems to be the first issue with which the Chamber is familiar already, because we have looked extensively to that report. Could you please be focussed and come to your point not after 20 minutes but immediately. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stojanovic, could you inform the Chamber about the Defence position in relation to the reconsideration of the decision on P1060?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Ivetic, will give you an answer in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, in relation to P1060 and the Prosecution motion for reconsideration, lead counsel, Mr. Lukic, has asked that we convey the Defence position that we oppose the motion for reconsideration in full and stand by our original objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I immediately give the decision of the Chamber. The Chamber hereby reconsiders the oral decision on admission of P1060 with regard to the entries related to the underlying documents indicated by the Prosecution in the informal communication dated the 25th of October. These entries are 3 through 8; 13; 15; 17; and 19 through 21. As stated in the Chamber's decision on the 23rd of October, the relevance and probative value are dependant on whether the underlying documents are in evidence. Therefore, the Chamber defers its decision on admission of the entries of the comment chart until the decision of admission of the underlying documents has been taken. The seven-day deadline granted on the 25th of October to the Prosecution for the military justice bar table reply is running as of today, the 28th of October. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meanwhile put on the record that our late start was due to technical problems with the transcribing system. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document D371 in e-court. Under 65 ter, it's marked 1D01289, and we need page 4 of this document. But before that, can we take a look at page number 1 so that we can see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter, and you can see it for yourself, Mr. Peccerelli, written by Dr. Moore to the Defence team of one of the accused in the Srebrenica case, which pertains to the excavations in the Lazete 2 that your report deals with. Now can we take a look together at the last paragraph on page 2 and part of page 3 of this report. So, first, let's look at this paragraph which has been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear what Ms. MacGregor would like to submit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Stojanovic characterises this as being -- line 18, it "pertains to the excavations in Lazete 2 that your report deals with." As I understand the document the Defence is using -- it relates to the excavations done at Lazete 2 in 1996. So just to be clear that what time-frame we're talking about that this document relates to, especially as the witness has already stated he knows very little about what happened in 1996 at that excavation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you agree that it's about the 1996 exhumations? Or excavations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours. That is correct, Your Honours. We are talking about 1996 exhumations, which are described in this letter, but it relates to this specific area, Lazete 2. Among other things, Dr. Moore says the following: That his impression was that digging out of human remains went very fast, even too fast because in some particular cases, all parts of the skeleton, for example, hands and feet that belonged the same person, were not put in the same bag due to the overcrowding of the grave and other bodies were in the way of accessing other bodies, or other parts of the bodies were not found due to disintegration. This could be the reason why these limbs had not been found. And he says: "I agree with Dr. Snow that only 20 bodies should be removed during a day."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in the procedures that you adopted from Professor Richard Wright, was the dynamic or the pace of your work laid down and the methodology to be applied in your work?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The methodology obviously was laid out, to a certain degree, but once you get into a grave, mass graves of this type tend to be complicated, and the bodies tend to overlap and intertwine. It is very difficult, and there is very little written about how to do it. However, we concentrate on maintaining the integrity of the body and in maximum recovery of the body. As far as the pace, I don't recall there being a specific part in the methodology that limits whether a low number or a high number of bodies per day. However, I do tend to agree with Dr. Clyde Snow, maybe not with the specific figure, but the fact that a manageable number for the team should be respected. To be able to recover each body and document each body properly is important during this -- the recovery process, and sometimes there have to be decisions made as far as why you would alter that. In other words, there have been times when I have heard in other instances where an exhumation team has recovered many bodies. This was in a well, and the walls were caving in, so they took many of the bodies out in a hurry, understanding that that would co-mingle the bodies; in other words, would not be easily identifiable. But, nonetheless there are instances where it is difficult or impossible to follow the proper methodology and logic behind it. Although, they should again -- maximum recovery of the evidence and the bodies is of the utmost concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can we be as brief as possible, and I'll be consistent and short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 2008 [as interpreted]. It concerns the San Antonio conference that we mentioned before the break. If we can have page 4, paragraph 5 of this report, and as I understand it, Professor Snow participated in this conference. Among other things, it says -- so page 4, item 5. That's paragraph of chapter 6, paragraph 5. It's the last one on the page, where Dr. Snow whilst commenting on the work of forensic experts on the ground says that, according to him, it was, quote/unquote, sloppy science. Would you agree that the work that had been done prior to your arrival could be described in this manner as Professor Snow put it, that is to say, as sloppy science.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find on the record that it is 65 ter number "2008," but it must be a mistake -- oh, it's 20008.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours. I believe that it should be 10 -- 120008.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question, Professor, is: Would you agree with this opinion of Professor Snow?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My interpretation of what was done at the site was that the methodology that we used in 2000 was very different than whatever was used in 1996. And this -- this is because of initially the surface finds, the lack of determination of one grave, the lack of determination of the size of the grave, as well as of the robbing incidents. However, I was not there, and I don't know the reason for this deviation from the standard methodology, and I would have to agree that when one reviews the result, it -- it does not appear to be consistent with proper methodology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain this. You say if you review the results. Where did you find the methodology not to be proper? What impropriety did you find?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, initially when we got there the first thing that we noticed is that a surface search had not been conducted and we were able to recover several hundred, if I'm not mistaken, 671 bullet casings among other ballistic evidence that were all lying on the surface of the field, not directly over the grave but on the field, and this is very standard. You initially -- before you begin to excavate into the ground, you're supposed to look on what's laying on the surface and how that relates to -- to -- to the grave itself. And I mean, I can continue, but among the other things is that the decision from what we found was to trench, which is a methodology used all over the world. However, the lack of determination of one larger grave shows a -- either a time constraint, personnel constraint, or lack of methodology to be able to follow the grave outline to understand the extent of the entire grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This flawed methodology that was dubbed by Professor Snow as sloppy science, does this allow a possibility for speculation that, for example, the cartridges that were discovered in situ in Lazete 2 that you spoke about, may not perhaps have been there in 1996 but due to whatever reason remained there or were used in the period between 1996 and 2000, which is the year when you came to the site?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I intervene here for a moment. In order to avoid sloppy fact-finding, the witness told us that because he found cartridges, surface examination, that it's either lack of time, lack of staff, or improper methodology. Now, your next question starts from a totally different point of view, although you started by saying, This flawed methodology. Now, if there were no cartridges in 1996, I think the witness would agree with us, that the fact that those cartridges were found later does not indicate flawed methodology because there was just nothing to recover at the time. So, therefore, linking the flawed methodology to putting the cartridges there later, are two totally different scenarios, and you are mixing them up in this one question. Would you please refrain from doing that and put your questions to the witness in such a way that such confusion will not appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to divide my question. Can you tell us, do you know or were you able to establish the time since those cartridges were in the area of Lazete?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In both cases, in Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, what we can say is that the cartridges were lying for an undetermined amount of time but enough time to be covered by secondary vegetation as well as about half a centimetre of soil. There is no specific, exact time-frame for that. However, it is prior to the time that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my next question is: On the basis of what you did in 2000, you're not able now to say whether those cartridges were there back in 1996 at all when the first works were being done on this grave.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I cannot make that estimation because the excavation did not contemplate the area where the cartridges were found. In other words, the 1996 excavations focussed very specifically on two areas of the grave which were -- I -- I need to see the map, but they were a distance away from where the majority of the -- of the bullet casings were found, or the ballistic evidence was found. However, I do have to say that it is difficult to make these determinations without taking the entire case into consideration. Each one of these cases, if you do ballistic analysis on them, can be traced to specific weapons, and there is also the same type of scenario in Lazete 1 as there is in Lazete 2. Lazete 1 had not been previously excavated by any other excavation team. So I think if we look at the entire scenario, we can probably make a better determination of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one related question. You earlier said it was bad methodology not to look to a surface because you found many cartridges there. If they had not been there in 1996 it would not be an indicator for bad methodology, therefore. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your judgement was a bit quick.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My judgement is based on Lazete 1. When we looked on the surface of Lazete 1, we found the cartridges cases. When we looked in Lazete 2, logic told us that these both were linked by many things, not just by the bullet casings, also by the scalloped pieces of material. And, again, this can be also looked at from afar by looking at the identification of the bodies and the specific time when these people were reported as missing individuals, so I think focussing on such a very specific area of it can lead us to make erroneous conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for Lazete 1, could you determine whether those cartridges had been there in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we could not determine a specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- period. We could determine they were there prior to our excavation, sometime. No specific time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So your judgement that it was flawed methodology for Lazete 1 was a quick and not fully founded judgement I -- as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lazete 1 was not previously excavated so there was no flawed methodology because there was nothing conducted on the site before. What I said was the possibility of there being this type of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But let me stop you there. Whatever happened before, merely on the basis of the fact that you found a lot of cartridges whether it would be Lazete 1 or Lazete 2, not knowing whether they had been there in 1996 does not allow for a judgement on flawed methodology on that basis. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm not making it only on that basis. I also mention time constraints, personnel constraints and also the way the grave was dug. I'm just using that as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there were no cartridge there in 1996, time restraint cannot explain why they were overlooked. Personnel restraints could not explain why they were overlooked. Therefore, I'm -- there is nothing wrong in just saying that the basis, the conclusions you drew there, are solely drawn on the basis of an assumption that the cartridges would have been there in 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The assumption is that the cartridges were there since July 1995. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was at the basis of your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this same document, let us take a look at page 10, item number 9, chapter entitled: Discussion and conclusions. I'm sorry, I think we need page 11 in English. That's the next page. There, the experts concerned, in line with the debates, says in assessment of the work done so far that there was too much subjectivity and lack of unbiased exhumations and post-mortem analysis. Does this conclusion stem from the fact that you mentioned earlier, and is that the ground on which you agreed with what Professor Snow said about the scientific methodology?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'll sorry, but I would have to read these one by one. And, once again, I had never seen this report before. My appreciation of the work done prior to our investigations is very specific to our appreciations. It is very difficult to make a determination on methodology used somewhere when I wasn't there in 1996 or -- if you'd like, you can read these. But obviously I didn't use any of these - I've never read them before - to make my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for your effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender document, which is the San Antonio report, which is 65 ter 20008. I'd like to have this admitted into evidence, and then I will proceed with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure there's been a clear foundation for the document laid. As this particular witness has stated over and over again, he's never seen this report before. He's not familiar with much of the process of writing it. So we'd object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as a bar table document, would you object as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tender it as a bar table document, Mr. Stojanovic? If you'd like to have it in evidence, that might be a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no problem with that. Technically speaking, that is an approach to take. Given the fact that the OTP is not opposed, we can tender it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I must say that I have a recollection that we have looked at it before. I do not -- my recollection doesn't tell me why it was not tendered or admitted at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, we'd like to -- or if any of the parties could assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. This document has been used before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It -- it -- could the parties assist me in -- in -- since I have a vivid recollection of this document, now find it, however, not to be tendered or at least not to be admitted, what the reason for that was before we decide now otherwise. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will meanwhile be marked for identification so as to find what exactly was said about it when Witness Haglund testified. Yes, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I think you just echoed what I am about to say which is we are trying to zone in -- write in when it was tendered but that our [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Twenty-four, 25th of July, if I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yeah. Was through Witness Haglund. And also the document that we were looking at just before this it looks like was already entered into evidence. So I think that also may be the familiarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have -- let's analyse -- let's try to find out what happened when we earlier looked at this document and have the document, meanwhile, be marked for identification. Madam Registrar, the number would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 20008 receives number D391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the casings that were found, do you know if they were ever analysed ballistically, as you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I do not have that information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will finish with these casings by asking if you were able to see the year of manufacture embossed on the casings.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Our -- our job was to document the evidence. There might be pictures. However, we did not analyse the evidence, and so -- however, I don't -- that's -- that's why it's not in the report because we did not analyse this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just been informed by my colleagues that the San Antonio report is an exhibit in this trial and has the -- bears the number D329. Therefore, I apologise for my motion to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, that seems to be the same document. It's a bit alarming if you prepare for cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic, that the Chamber has a better recollection of the evidence presented by the Defence than the Defence itself has. But please proceed, meanwhile. The last number assigned, which was D391, is vacated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, why did I ask you all those questions about methodology? When you came to the field and were introduced to the area of Lazete 1 and 2, were you able to observe the exact localities where the PHR excavated the grave-sites in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If I may, when I got to Lazete 1, there was no intent of going into Lazete 2, so we did not -- we were not instructed or were not shown the site, at all. It wasn't until later, if I remember correctly, August the 2nd, which was almost towards the end of the investigation of Lazete 1, did I receive a phone call asking me to please go look at the area on the other side of the train tracks, which was named Lazete 2. On initial inspection, we could not see the areas that PHR had exhumed. However, after scraping the surface, off the -- over the ground, over the grave, we were able to see that the grave was expanded very specifically in two areas. These two areas are called Lazete 2A and B in my report. And our excavation is referred to as Lazete 2C, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How much time elapsed from the moment you started working or possibly finished working on Lazete 1 to the moment you started working on Lazete 2C?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We started working on Lazete 1 on July 13th. So you just have to calculate something like three weeks before we started working on Lazete 2C. And there was an overlap of six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To make things perfectly clear, let me ask you if Lazete 2A and Lazete 2B are physically separate graves that were excavated by the -- by the previous investigative team in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: After conducting the investigation there, my conclusion is that graves -- as they were called, 2A and 2B - were not separate graves but were body concentrations inside of a larger grave, which we called Lazete 2C.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the Lazete 2C grave excavated in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Not completely. Two parts of Lazete 2C were excavated only, not the entire grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which technique was used to fill the graves after those first works back in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: From the look of it, they were filled in with machinery because of the type of soil and the way the soil was arranged. But we couldn't really tell much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us together look at document P2523 [as interpreted], pages -- page 3 in both languages. It's a summary of your report for Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 2523, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2553. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor, focus on spots (h) and (i), or, rather, items (h) and (i) where you say concerning the situation that the PHR team exhumed two clusters of bodies within a large grave but they did not excavate the entire grave. Here's my question: Do you know, or were you told when you began to work on Lazete 2, that there were bodies there that had been uncovered and then buried again by the previous investigative team in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: On the initial phone call, I was told that there was a team member from 1996 that had reported that there was some bodies left behind. But that's -- that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was any mention of the time during which those bodies were uncovered - that is, exposed to weather - in 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall when that exhumation occurred, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told at any point or possibly I misunderstood when that exhumation was done. In your item (f), you state that: "In 1996, the PHR exhumation team conducted an investigation at this site..."

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I obviously put in it was 1996. But you asked whether I knew when in 1996, and I don't know when in 1996. I know it was during 1996 at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether, at any point before you began to excavate Lazete 2 you had information about the duration of time during which the bodies were exposed to the elements; that is, uncovered.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Since there was three previous interventions on this grave, you need to clarify when you're talking about. Because there was the initial excavation of the grave; there was a later -- what we call robbing of the grave; and then there was a later excavation by the PHR team. I'm not sure if you're referring to any of those two previous ones or if you're only referring to the PHR team. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that is exactly what I mean, the excavation conducted by the PHR in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could I then -- Mr. Stojanovic, just to understand everything, are you referring to the bodies that were left behind, how long they had been exposed to the -- to the elements? Is that what you're asking? Let's then first clarify what the witness told us. You said that you heard from one member of the 1996 team that some bodies were left behind. Did -- was this ever corroborated by other reports or other persons, or was that your one and only source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my one and own source but it was a secondary source. I never spoke to this team member. I was only told this by investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second-hand hearsay, therefore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There you go, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did that information that bodies were left behind include anything as to whether these bodies were ever been brought to the surface and exposed to the elements or whether they were -- it was a message that not all the bodies that, most likely, there were more bodies still to be exhumed there? Was there any such information part of that second-hand hearsay evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my understanding, what I gathered, was that the investigators had knowledge that there was more bodies in the grave and therefore that's the reason why they wanted to go and get the rest of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But whether they had already been exposed to the elements, was that part of that information that they were or were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not. Although, if you understand what this secondary information when a team members says that they saw another body, probably means, from what I understand, in one of the walls of the grave, and part of it probably was exposed. But, again, this is -- I wasn't there. It's very difficult to understand what this person saw from my point of view. I went in there to recover the rest of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, I'm asking these questions because you -- your questions started on the assumption that the bodies which were left behind were exposed to the elements, which was not yet established. And I -- from the latest answer of the witness, it's even likely that he'll not be able to answer such questions, not even through hearsay. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your help, Your Honours. This is what I had supposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But please tell me once more whether at any point you had indirect information about the number of bodies that had remained in Lazete 2 after the end of the work of the PHR team in 1996.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We did not have any prior knowledge to the amount of bodies that could have been left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, taking into consideration your experience and your work on this site - I'm referring to Lazete 2 - can you tell us how many times this grave, after the initial excavation and the burial of the bodies therein, was opened and filled in again?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The grave was opened twice after the initial excavation of the grave, prior to our excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me whether, in your opinion, the bodies there were the result of primary burial, or is it something else? I'm referring to the 16 bodies found at Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The 16 bodies we found were -- well, comprised a primary mass grave. The result: They were there because they were very close to the walls, and during a robbing excavation of those areas, those bodies were missed. However, they were found in situ in the original location that they had been buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I again try to carefully look at what the evidence at this moment is. I take you back to one of your previous questions, Mr. Stojanovic. You asked, in relation to Lazete 2: "Can you tell us how many times this grave, after the initial excavation and the burial of the bodies therein, was opened and filled in again." The word "excavation" was used. Today, that word has been used in a different way as well, as "exhumation." Did you mean to say, to ask, how many times the graves was opened after the burial of the first persons in that grave were deposited there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is why -- let us clarify. This -- I don't consider this first digging instance an exhumation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then let's carefully look at what the witness then told us. The witness said: "The grave was opened twice after the initial excavation of the grave." Could you, Witness, be precise on what instances you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the initial instance is the moment when the ground was dug up, and at that point it was a hole in the ground. When bodies were deposited into it, it became a grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first you mentioned or did you start from that point in time [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first one I mentioned, and that, if you look at the images we have a date for, it is between July 5th and July 27th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, that grave was opened twice. Once during the robbing excavations; and the second time, during the PHR excavation and exhumation process, as part of the investigation; and, finally, a -- a third time, when we got there in -- in 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer is three times instead of two. But because the question is unclear as to what is the starting point. I do understand now that initially a hole was dug in the earth, bodies were put in there, the grave was filled again, then it was once re-opened at what we call the instance of the grave being robbed, filled again, after that, the 1996 exhumation which was incomplete, and then your work, which is then the fourth time or the third time after the grave was dug.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's no confusion now anymore. Mr. Stojanovic, we take a break. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, but not until after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, we had a few delays, and especially in the start of the second series but we are now late as well, and -- I wouldn't say that the Chamber apologises for it, but I do apologise for it. That's not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I do as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, two apologies. Mr. Stojanovic, in terms of time, do you think that we will be able to conclude the testimony of this witness this morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I reckon I will need one hour more, and I have notified the OTP about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Ms. MacGregor, that would leave you sufficient time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we dealt with Lazete 2C and the exhumation of 16 bodies bound in that grave. My next question is: Can you tell us, were you able, at any point, on the basis of your expertise, the time of death of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To determine the time of death of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time of death was not a determination that the field team had to make. That would be a determination that would take place in the lab. The information we had pertains specifically to the images of when the grave was created and filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the images that you had at your disposal, these graves were created, as you said, between the 5th of July and the 27th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly move away from the microphone slightly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These aerial images do not provide any information whatsoever about the time when the bodies were deposited in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, looking at these images, I could tell you the answer. Of course, they do not say anything. They give one picture, the 5th; one picture, 27th. Whether the bodies were put there after the 27th or before the 27th, but likely not after the 5th, that's obvious from the material which you have gone through again and again in view of many graves. Please proceed. Unless the witness would disagree with me. You have listened to me. I see you're nodding no. No disagreement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor, the artefacts you discovered in Lazete 2C, who were they passed on to for further analysis?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: All the evidence recovered at the scene was given to the scene-of-crime officer and, from my understanding, handed over to the morgue in Visoko or the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information at any point about the commission that worked in 1996, how many bodies they had dug out at the time?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I do not recall having that information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now have a photograph from P1132 in e-court, marked in e-court 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, do you recognise this area, especially on the left-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes. That appears to be the field where the Lazete 1 grave was found. The picture appears to be taken from the train tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with your recollection that this area marked with an ellipsis is exactly the area where you located Lazete 1?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Exactly, no; but it's in the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You had never been told that any of the ICTY investigators prior to your arrival did anything in connection with exhumations in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I was not told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for your work, did it lead you to believe and/or to determine as to how many times this particular grave had been opened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object. There's no foundation laid to establish why he's -- why the witness is being asked about Lazete 1 being previously excavated, which is what I understand this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, does this trigger you to rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, I'm looking at your report on Lazete 1, and I wanted to ask you this: In the course of your work regarding the exhumations in Lazete 1, did you establish that this grave had been disturbed?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: May I look at my report, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may. Unless the Prosecution has any objections to it. No. Please look at your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I can also ask that we have now P2552, pages 4 -- or, rather, page 3 in both versions, and this will clarify the direction and the line of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document is on the screen, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honours. I'm just waiting for the professor to take a look at his notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, I'm going to ask you this -- or, rather, repeat my question. Taking into account what is written here - I will not repeat myself - now, in the course of your work at Lazete 1, was it possible to draw any conclusions as to how many this particular area had been re-excavated or re-exhumed prior to the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We had other aerial images, figures 14A and 14B of the report on page 11, which give us a close-up to the field of where Lazete 1 is located. And what we can see there, there's an image again dated September 7 1995 when we can see an oval shape with some clear edges and then that next to it there's an image dating September 27 1995. The images of the oval shape have been extended. The borders of the oval shape had been extended. There's a track --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we -- was it page 11?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 11 on the written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the relevant page. I do not know whether page 11 is also e-court 11. Could you look at your screen whether that is one of the pictures you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next page, one page further, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the close-up would have to be in the second line of images. There. So looking at this image, what we thought happened was that the grave was re-opened at some point, and can you see the track marks leading from the grave to the main road and also from the grave to the dirt track on the side. This was supported when we exhumed the grave by two areas that were located within the grave called robbing area A and robbing area B where most body parts were located and also at the edges where truncated bodies were also located. So with the initial hypothesis drawn from these images and then later with the physical evidence drawn from the grave, I ascertained that the grave was reopened between the dates of 7th September, 1995, and the 27th of September, 1995, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I ask one clarifying question. Is there any way to determine whether that has been a one-time occasion or whether it may have happened even more than one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the locations within the grave, if the exhumations, if the extraction of the bodies was smaller than the original, it could have happened more than once. However, what we see is clear borders of an extraction of bodies. These could have been done on separate days but it could have been on the same day, but there's two areas. And from the images, we gather that they occurred between those dates but we cannot say if it was a single event or if it was two.
